title: "Dealing with positive controls"

---

This section documents how to inspect positive controls to confirm successful amplification of target genes, detect false results, and overall, verify that the full workflow (from extraction to bioinformatics) behaves as expected [@lear2018].

To follow the example presented on this page directly on your computer, download the script `003_positive_control.R` and the example raw data by clicking the buttons below. Alternatively, you may copy the codes below into your own script, and use your own data.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
library(downloadthis)
library(phyloseq)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
load("../../RData/ITS/otu_table_raw.RData")
```

```{r}
#| layout: [[-10,35,-5,40,-10]]
#| echo: false
download_file(
  path = "../../scripts/ITS/003_positive_control.R",
  output_name = "003_positive_control",
  button_label = "Download script",
  button_type = "success",
  has_icon = TRUE,
  icon = "fa fa-save",
  self_contained = FALSE
)

download_file(
  path = "../../RData/ITS/otu_table_raw.RData",
  output_name = "ITS_otu_table_raw",
  button_label = "Download example RData",
  button_type = "success",
  has_icon = TRUE,
  icon = "fa fa-save",
  self_contained = FALSE
)
```

### Inspect samples

Positive controls added before sequencing usually contain a synthetic community (OTUs absent from true samples) and serve to demonstrate successful amplification of target genes or provide information about tag-switching. In this example, the positive controls contain a synthetic ITS sequence (a "spike-in"), which is assigned to the kingdom `Unispike1` in the taxonomy table.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Load raw OTU table
load("RData/ITS/otu_table_raw.RData")
```

To inspect this data set, convert OTU table from count data to both a presence-absence table and a relative abundance table.

```{r}
# Convert OTU table from count data to presence-absence
otu_table.pa <- transform_sample_counts(otu_table_raw, function(x) 1*(x>0))

# Convert OTU table from count data to relative abundance
otu_table.rel <- transform_sample_counts(otu_table_raw, function(x) x/sum(x))
```

#### Identify synthetic community

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 6
# Identify OTUs present in positive controls
otu_table.pa.pos <- prune_samples(
  sample_data(otu_table.pa)$sample_type == "positive control", otu_table.pa)

table.pa.pos <- data.frame(pa.pos = taxa_sums(otu_table.pa.pos))

otu_pos <- filter(table.pa.pos, pa.pos > 0) %>% rownames()

# Filter OTU table to keep only OTUs found in positive controls
otu_table_pos <- prune_taxa(otu_pos, otu_table.rel)

# Visualize the abundance of these OTUs in all samples
p_pos_otus <- plot_bar(otu_table_pos, fill = "kingdom") +
  facet_grid(~sample_type, scales = "free", space = "free")
p_pos_otus
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Save the plot in the figures folder
ggsave("figures/ITS/003_pos_control_otus_relative_abundance.png", p_pos_otus,
       width = 12, height = 6)
```

Nearly all reads in the two positive controls (385 and 817 reads) belong to the spike-in (`Unispike1`), as expected. The positive controls also contain a few reads (1 to 2 per OTU) of soil fungi, such as the ectomycorrhizal genera *Cortinarius* and *Inocybe*, which most likely come from the true samples. These cross-contaminations can be dealt with using the R package `decontam`, as demonstrated in the next section: [Dealing with negative controls](controls-negative.qmd).

The spike-in is absent from the true samples, so there was no contamination from the positive controls into the samples. The spike-in will be automatically removed from our data set while performing [taxonomic filtering](filter.qmd), which keeps only Fungi.

#### Compare community profiles

If one suspects issues with library preparation or sequencing, positive controls can be used for visual inspection, by making sure the taxonomic profiles match expectations.

```{r}
#| warning: false
# Keep only positive controls for visualization
otu_table.rel.pos <- prune_samples(
  sample_data(otu_table.rel)$sample_type == "positive control", otu_table.rel)

# Visualize the community profiles of these samples
p_pos_profiles <- plot_bar(otu_table.rel.pos, fill = "kingdom")
p_pos_profiles
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
ggsave("figures/ITS/003_pos_control_profiles.png", p_pos_profiles,
       width = 7, height = 5)
```

Both positive controls show the same profile, dominated by the spike-in: no obvious issue was detected during library preparation or sequencing.

### Clean and save OTU table

Since no issue was detected, the positive controls can simply be removed from the data set.

::: callout-tip
## remove_taxa

Homemade function `remove_taxa`: a simplified way of removing a selection of OTU from a `phyloseq` object.

```{r}
#| eval: false
remove_taxa <- function(badTaxa, physeq){
  allTaxa <- taxa_names(physeq)
  cleanTaxa <- allTaxa[!(allTaxa %in% badTaxa)]
  return(prune_taxa(cleanTaxa, physeq))
}
```
:::

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Remove positive controls
otu_ctrl_pos_clean <- prune_samples(
  sample_data(otu_table_raw)$sample_type != "positive control", otu_table_raw)

# Save cleaned OTU table
save(otu_ctrl_pos_clean, file = "RData/ITS/otu_ctrl_pos_clean.RData")
```
